newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FORECAST - Think-tank turns more bullish on Hungary.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Think-tank turns more bullish on Hungary.

text.p: Hungary's independent economic think-tank GKI Gazdasagkutato Rt said on Wednesday it revised its earlier forecasts for 1997 inflation down and for GDP and real wage growth up.
The research institute lowered its forecast for the average inflation rate for 1997 to 18.5 percent from 19.5 percent in its forecast in March.

"This is the result of the fact that inflation was somewhat lower in all of the first four months, especially in the first quarter of the year than our earlier forecasts," Andras Vertes, GKI Managing Director told a news conference.
Hungary's monthly and year-on-year consumer inflation rates showed a declining trend over the past 18 months.

The Central Statistical Office (KSH) registered a monthly CPI index of 3.7 percent in January, 2.2 percent in February, 1.9 percent in March and 1.4 percent in April 1997, while the year-on-year indices were 18.9 percent, 18.8 percent, 18.8 percent and 18.6 percent, respectively.

Hungary wants to reduce average inflation to 13 to 14 percent in 1998 from a forecast 18 percent this year and December year-on-year CPI would fall to 11 to 12 percent in 1998 from a projected 16 to 17 percent in 1997.

GKI expected a further fall in the May year-on-year inflation figure, to be followed by a slight rise in CPI indices in the subsequent three months due to an increase in prices of seasonal products, Vertes said.

"The pace of (monthly) inflation will fall substantially in May compared to May last year," he said, adding that the rise in the summer months will stem from the fact that comparative price levels were very low in the same period of 1996.
GKI revised its predictions for Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) upwards, to three percent from 2.5 percent earlier, Vertes said.
"We regard industry an area where growth will be slightly higher than we thought earlier," he said. "In services, we see a slight increase against the earlier forecast of stagnation."
Vertes said the economic growth was driven mainly by investment and exports, but also by consumption.
The government targets an increase in GDP of two to three percent.
The think-tank revised its forecasts for real wages and consumption upwards after heavy wage increases in the administration sector earlier this year.

"The starting level of wages was much higher than we predicted earlier, therefore we expect real wages to rise by nearly five percent, compared to our forecast in March of around three percent," Vertes said.
As a result real incomes and household consumption will be higher than earlier expected, he said, adding that GKI forecast a two to three percent rise in consumption for 1997.
